I'm also cataloging the branch behaviors for add, addAll, set, remove, removeAll, and retainAll -- tracking cases like duplicate detection, index shifts during batch adds, position matching in set(), and how removals sync back to the underlying set.

I'm noting the inner iterator classes too, especially the ListIterator's contains-check on add and the UnsupportedOperationException thrown by set(). Adding tests to verify subList returns a SetUniqueList and that adding a duplicate already present in the parent list gets rejected, since the sublist shares the same uniqueness set. Now I want to reexamine the scenario where an object already exists but at a different index to make sure that edge case is handled correctly.

I trace through setting index 0 to "c" when "c" already exists later in the list — the position found doesn't match the target index, so after the assignment I need to remove the stale duplicate entry and clean it from the tracking set, which matches my expected outcome. I also verify the same-position case leaves the list untouched since no duplicate removal is needed, and the case where the new value doesn't exist anywhere in the list simply proceeds without needing any cleanup.

Now I trace through addAll(int, Collection) when duplicates already exist mid-list: adding "a" gets skipped since it's already tracked in the set, so the index doesn't advance, but adding "b" succeeds and inserts properly, shifting the index forward — the final list matches my expectation. I then walk through a second addAll test where both "b" and "c" are new insertions, confirming each addition increments the index correctly as the list grows.

I also verify the sublist implementation shares the same underlying set with its parent list, so duplicate checks apply consistently across both views — adding an already-present element via the sublist correctly gets ignored. And the "asSet is unmodifiable" test should hold since UnmodifiableSet naturally throws on mutation attempts, consistent with its naming and typical decorator behavior.

Tracing through decorate with duplicate elements like [a,b,a,c], I confirm the algorithm correctly builds a fresh set, clears the list, then re-adds each element one by one via addAll — skipping "a" the second time since the set already contains it, while properly incrementing the index for genuinely new elements.

This gives a final list of [a,b,c], matching my earlier expectation and the test's assertions exactly.

I also reconsider the null-set test on the protected constructor: since decorate() always supplies a fresh HashSet and subList() always passes the existing non-null field, there's no public path to trigger the null check, so reflection is genuinely necessary here and I'll keep that test as-is.

Checking testAddAllEmptyCollection, the loop over an empty collection never executes so sizeBefore equals size() and it returns false, which matches expectations. I've now covered both branches of the hasNext loop and the sizeBeforeAddNext comparison, plus true/false branches for containsAll/removeAll/retainAll, so this set feels comprehensive -- though I might add an out-of-bounds test for subList as a boundary check, even though behavior is likely just delegated to the underlying list.

I'm also adding tests for negative index and out-of-bounds removal that expect IndexOutOfBoundsException, relying on standard ArrayList contract behavior. Then I'm adding a null-element test to verify HashSet/ArrayList null handling and duplicate detection, followed by an empty-list test checking size and failed removals.

With the suite feeling solid, I realize I can place the test class in the same package as the source so the protected constructor becomes directly accessible without needing reflection — a much cleaner approach typical of Defects4J-style test setups. That lets me write a constructor test expecting IllegalArgumentException when passed a null set directly.

I confirm dependent classes like AbstractIteratorDecorator and UnmodifiableSet are already available on the project's classpath since they're part of the same library, so I don't need to worry about extra imports. Now I'm finalizing the test file with the correct package declaration and direct instantiation for the constructor test.

I'll match the source code's use of raw types (List, Set, Collection) rather than generics, consistent with this pre-generics era of the Collections library. Finalizing the code now.
